target.title: fix(telegram): distinguish and render streamed reasoning/commentary progress lanes
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves Fixes an issue where Telegram users watching a streamed reply saw **no formatting at all** in the live progress draft: reasoning and commentary were indistinguishable (no lane markers, both plain), and the model's Markdown (`**`, backticks, `_…_`) either leaked as literal characters or was silently stripped. Three stacked defects, found by driving a live bot and inspecting the exact payloads: 1. **No lane identity.** The Telegram channel never passed the compositor's per-channel lane markers, so reasoning and commentary rendered identically (Discord passes 🧠/💬 and renders reasoning italic, commentary plain). 2. **Wrong renderer for lane text.** Progress lane bodies were hand-escaped rather than Markdown-rendered, so `**bold**`/backticks leaked raw; long reasoning lines additionally lost their closing `_` to truncation and degraded from italic to plain. 3. **`
` broke every multi-line preview at the transport.** Progress drafts join rendered lines with `
`, but Bot API `parse_mode=HTML` has no `
` tag — Telegram rejected every multi-line preview edit with "can't parse entities", and the parse-error fallback silently downgraded the whole draft to unformatted plain text. Because of this, streamed progress formatting effectively **never rendered** on non-rich Telegram accounts, whatever the payload said. ## Why This Change Was Made Three focused fixes, one per commit: 1. **Lane rendering** — pass the `🧠`/`💬` lane prefixes and `commentaryItalics: false` to the shared progress-draft compositor (mirroring the Discord channel), and render lane bodies through `renderTelegramHtmlText` (the `parse_mode=HTML`-safe converter). Lane lines collapse to one line first — multi-line commentary otherwise forms block markdown (a `\n\n---\n\n` separator turns the paragraph above it into a setext `

`, which Telegram rejects). Long lines clip *inside* the whole-line `_…_` wrapper so truncation can't chop the closing underscore. 2. **Transport** — convert `
` joins to literal newlines in the `parse_mode=HTML` transport branch, matching what the rich-message branch already does. 3. **Preview lifetime** — keep the streaming preview on screen ≥4s from first appearance before a teardown delete, scheduled detached (never awaited) so turn teardown is not stalled; on fast turns the box otherwise flashed away unread, and the immediate delete could race a just-persisted message. Non-goals: final-answer rendering and the durable (`/verbose on`) lanes are untouched — this is only the streamed progress window. ## User Impact Telegram users watching a streamed reply now see a formatted progress draft for the first time: reasoning (🧠, *italic*) clearly distinct from commentary (💬, plain), with the model's Markdown rendered — bold step names, monospace commands — instead of leaking or being stripped, and the progress box stays readable on fast turns. Biggest improvement for deepseek, which narrates progress almost entirely through its markdown-heavy reasoning lane. ## Evidence **Live capture** (dev gateway on this branch, Telegram Desktop, anthropic sonnet, `/reasoning stream`, fresh session). Same turn, in order: Reasoning lane — `🧠` + italic, with the model's `**bold**` rendered bold-italic and backtick commands in monospace, all inside the italic wrapper: ![reasoning zoom](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Marvinthebored/openclaw/proof-assets-telegram-progress-lanes/telegram-streamed-progress-lanes/pr-proof-2b-reasoning-zoom.png) Commentary lane — `💬` + upright, bold step names, monospace commands (contrast with the italic reasoning above): ![commentary zoom](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Marvinthebored/openclaw/proof-assets-telegram-progress-lanes/telegram-streamed-progress-lanes/pr-proof-3b-commentary-zoom.png) Full-stage frames: [prompt](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Marvinthebored/openclaw/proof-assets-telegram-progress-lanes/telegram-streamed-progress-lanes/pr-proof-1-prompt.png) · [🧠 reasoning](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Marvinthebored/openclaw/proof-assets-telegram-progress-lanes/telegram-streamed-progress-lanes/pr-proof-2-reasoning-italic.png) · [💬 commentary](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Marvinthebored/openclaw/proof-assets-telegram-progress-lanes/telegram-streamed-progress-lanes/pr-proof-3-commentary.png) · [💬 step 3](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Marvinthebored/openclaw/proof-assets-telegram-progress-lanes/telegram-streamed-progress-lanes/pr-proof-4-commentary2.png) · [final](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Marvinthebored/openclaw/proof-assets-telegram-progress-lanes/telegram-streamed-progress-lanes/pr-proof-5-final.png) **Why the transport fix is required:** before it, the exact same preview payload was rejected by Telegram (`
` in `parse_mode=HTML`) and the live bubble showed the stripped plain fallback — verified by driving the intermediate build, which rendered everything plain despite a correct payload. **Before payload** (current `main`, same input, captured through the real dispatch): both lanes italic, no markers, raw markdown leaking — ```html Barnacling
Running `date`, then reading AGENTS.md
**Step 1: Running `date`.** ``` **Tests** — `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/telegram/src/bot-message-dispatch.test.ts extensions/telegram/src/draft-stream.test.ts` → **198 passed**. New coverage: markdown rendering in both lanes, clipped-long-reasoning stays italic, multi-line commentary stays `parse_mode`-safe (the setext-`

` trap), `
`→newline transport conversion, and the ≥4s dwell timing.

target.title: fix(codex): guard sandbox http/request JSON.parse against non-JSON stdout
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`runSandboxHttpRequest` in `extensions/codex/src/app-server/sandbox-exec-server/http.ts` parsed the sandbox shell helper's stdout with an unguarded `JSON.parse` (line 91). When the helper exits 0 but emits non-JSON (startup banner, debug log interleaved with the response, stdout truncated by `maxBuffer`, or SIGPIPE), the raw `SyntaxError` bubbled up to the JSON-RPC dispatcher as an opaque error (`Unexpected token ...`) with no mention of `sandbox http/request`, making root-cause hard to identify.

## Why This Change Was Made

Same `JSON.parse` guard pattern shipped this week across matrix (#97973), sms (#97999), signal (#98073), plugin-sdk (#98125), telegram ingress (#98372), and qmd mcporter (#98381). The streaming sibling in this same file (`runStreamingSandboxHttpRequest`) already wraps each stdout line via `requireObject(JSON.parse(line))`; the non-streaming path was missed.

The thrown message is kept generic on purpose. `JSON.parse`'s `SyntaxError` embeds a snippet of the raw input, which is surfaced before session visibility filtering; placing that snippet on the thrown Error (or on `.cause`, which `formatErrorMessage` walks into the user-visible path) would leak raw sandbox stdout. The guard throws a typed, attributable error with a generic message instead.

## User Impact

A Codex `http/request` tool whose sandbox helper emits non-JSON stdout now fails with a clear `sandbox http/request returned non-JSON stdout` error instead of an opaque `Unexpected token ...` SyntaxError. Valid JSON responses and the happy path are unchanged.

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior addressed:** A non-JSON sandbox helper stdout (exit 0) threw a raw `SyntaxError` out of `runSandboxHttpRequest`, surfaced by the JSON-RPC dispatcher as an opaque error with no sandbox context.
- **Real environment tested:** Linux x86_64, Node v24.14.0, commit `935aa82dab` on branch `fix/codex-sandbox-http-jsonparse-guard`.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:** `node --import tsx verify-codex-sandbox-http-real.mjs` — drives the real exported `httpRequest` JSON-RPC handler over a real exec-server WebSocket (replicating `sandbox-exec-server.test-helpers.ts` without the vitest `vi` dependency). Only the sandbox shell backend is mocked (there is no real sandbox helper in CI); `httpRequest -> runSandboxHttpRequest -> JSON.parse` runs for real. The backend returns `{code: 0, stdout: "<html>daemon warning</html>"}` and the script issues `initialize` then `http/request`.
- **Evidence after fix:** Terminal capture of `node` runtime verification (live stdout, copied verbatim — real exec-server, real WebSocket JSON-RPC):

  ```text
  $ node --import tsx verify-codex-sandbox-http-real.mjs
  drives the real httpRequest JSON-RPC path over a real exec-server WebSocket;
  only the sandbox shell backend is mocked (no real sandbox helper exists in CI).

  [agent/embedded] codex sandbox exec-server started

  backend returned: code=0, stdout='<html>daemon warning</html>' (non-JSON)
  http/request rejected -> error.message = "sandbox http/request returned non-JSON stdout"

  Verdict: real httpRequest path surfaces a typed 'non-JSON stdout' error (bug fixed)
  ```

- **Observed result after fix:** The real `httpRequest` JSON-RPC path rejects with `sandbox http/request returned non-JSON stdout` when the sandbox helper returns a non-JSON stdout at exit 0, instead of an opaque SyntaxError. The error is attributable (`sandbox http/request`) and carries no raw stdout snippet.
- **What was not tested:** A real sandboxed shell helper emitting a daemon banner over a live network call (the sandbox helper has an SSRF guard that blocks loopback/private IPs, so a local HTTP server is not a faithful stand-in; the real exec-server + mocked shell backend is the closest non-mocked reproduction of the `httpRequest -> runSandboxHttpRequest` decision boundary). Valid-JSON regression is covered by `sandbox-exec-server.http.test.ts` (8 tests, incl. `routes HTTP requests through the sandbox backend`).

## Tests and validation

```text
$ pnpm test extensions/codex/src/app-server/sandbox-exec-server.http.test.ts
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  8 passed (8)
```

Added `surfaces a typed error when the sandbox helper returns non-JSON stdout`: drives the real `httpRequest` JSON-RPC path with a mocked sandbox backend that returns a 0-exit non-JSON stdout, and asserts the rejection matches `/non-JSON stdout/i`.

## Risk checklist

- User-visible behavior: Yes (intended, bounded) - a non-JSON sandbox helper stdout now surfaces a typed, attributable error instead of an opaque SyntaxError; valid JSON and the happy path unchanged.
- Config/env/migration behavior: No - no config or env surface touched.
- Security/auth/secrets/network/tool execution: Yes (improvement) - the thrown message is generic and does not embed raw sandbox stdout or the SyntaxError raw-input snippet; no new credential, network, or command-execution path.
- Plugins/providers/channels/SDK: No - internal to the Codex sandbox exec-server; `runSandboxHttpRequest` keeps its return type.
- Highest-risk area: a future sandbox helper change that legitimately prints non-JSON to stdout on success - but that is exactly the case the guard makes attributable instead of opaque.
- Mitigation: 8 http tests (incl. the new non-JSON-stdout case) + node runtime verification driving the real `httpRequest` JSON-RPC path over a real exec-server WebSocket.

Closes: N/A (no existing issue)

target.title: docs(irc): document missing mentionPatterns config field
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`extensions/irc/src/config-schema.ts` defines `mentionPatterns` (an array of custom regex strings) at the account level, but `docs/channels/irc.md` does not list it as a config key. Users configuring IRC cannot discover this field from the docs.

- Problem: The `mentionPatterns` field exists in the IRC config schema and types but is absent from the access-control config key reference
- Solution: Add a `mentionPatterns` entry to the config key list in the Access control section
- What changed: `docs/channels/irc.md` (+1 line — one config key bullet)
- What did NOT change: No code or behavior changes. Documentation only.

## Evidence

### Schema (`extensions/irc/src/config-schema.ts:66`)

```typescript
mentionPatterns: z.array(z.string()).optional(),
```

### Runtime type (`extensions/irc/src/types.ts:57`)

```typescript
mentionPatterns?: string[];
```

### Runtime consumer — mention resolution (`extensions/irc/src/inbound.ts:224`)

```typescript
const mentionRegexes = core.channel.mentions.buildMentionRegexes(config as OpenClawConfig);
```

The IRC inbound handler builds mention regexes from the full channel config, which includes `mentionPatterns`. When set, these custom patterns override the default nick-based mention matching.

### Runtime consumer — channel policy resolver (`src/channels/mention-pattern-policy.ts:58`)

```typescript
const policy = isRecord(channelConfig) ? channelConfig.mentionPatterns : undefined;
```

The core channel framework reads `mentionPatterns` from each channel's config to resolve mention-pattern policies.

## User Impact

Users can now discover the `mentionPatterns` config field from the IRC docs. This is particularly useful for IRC setups with non-standard nick formats or keyword-based triggering requirements.

target.title: fix(matrix): reverse-proxy path support for Matrix homeserver URLs
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Matrix channel connections fail for homeservers deployed behind reverse proxies with path prefixes (e.g., `https://host/proxy/base/`). The previous implementation incorrectly constructed transport URLs by using absolute paths, causing `new URL()` to strip the reverse-proxy path prefix and resolve only against the origin.

Users deploying Matrix homeservers in containerized environments, FaaS platforms, or any setup requiring a reverse-proxy path prefix would experience connection failures even with valid credentials and network access.

## Why This Change Was Made

The fix moves URL construction entirely to the transport layer by ensuring endpoints are resolved relative to the full homeserver base path. The `apiPrefix` config surface was removed following ClawSweeper review as it was not carried through the runtime (`resolveMatrixConfigForAccount`, `MatrixAuth`, client keying, or `createMatrixClient`), making it a no-op for normal paths.

Key changes:
- `transport.ts`: `normalizeEndpoint()` strips leading slashes so `new URL(endpoint, baseUrl)` resolves relative to the full base path; `performMatrixRequest()` ensures the homeserver URL ends with `/` so it's treated as a directory
- `http-client.ts`: Replaced public `apiPrefix` parameter with private `DEFAULT_API_PREFIX` constant for bare-path resolution only
- Removed unused `apiPrefix` from `MatrixClient` constructor, config schema, and types

This approach keeps the fix minimal and transport-local without introducing new config surfaces that would require migration, validation, and lifecycle management.

## Linked context

- Fixes reverse-proxy path prefix resolution for Matrix channel connections
- No related open issues found
- No known affected releases (config was never shipped)

## User Impact

Matrix channel users running homeservers behind reverse proxies with path prefixes (e.g., `https://host/proxy/base/`) can now successfully connect and communicate. Previously, these deployments would fail during transport URL construction because the leading slash in endpoint paths caused `new URL()` to resolve against the origin only, stripping the proxy path.

No action required from existing users—this is a transparent fix. No new config options were added; instead, an unused `apiPrefix` config surface was removed as part of narrowing the scope.

## Real behavior proof (required for external PRs)

- **Behavior addressed**: Matrix channel fails to connect when the homeserver URL includes a reverse-proxy path prefix (e.g., https://host/proxy/base/).
- **Real environment tested**: Linux x64, Node 24.13.1, target homeserver behind openresty reverse proxy with path prefix.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch**: Configured Matrix channel with path-prefixed homeserver URL, started gateway, opened Control UI, navigated to Channels page.
- **Evidence after fix**:
  ![Matrix Channel Status](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/7802eb0e-418e-4b58-8022-ee5a2126dd8b)
  ![Matrix Channel Configuration](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/058e949b-862c-4bde-a618-cdf2618e4f60)
- **Observed result after fix**: Matrix channel shows connected status with healthy transport. No URL construction errors in gateway logs.

## Tests and validation

- 1393 tests passed (121 test files) in `extensions/matrix/`
- Standard homeserver URLs (`https://matrix.example.org`) continue to work correctly — verified with and without trailing slash
- Path-prefixed homeserver URLs now resolve correctly
- No regressions in existing Matrix channel functionality

## Risk checklist

**Compatibility**: 
- ✅ Config `apiPrefix` was never shipped to any release — no existing users affected
- ✅ Standard homeserver URLs unaffected — backward compatible URL resolution
- ✅ Migration not needed — config surface removed before any release

**Message delivery**:  
- ✅ Transport-only change — only affects HTTP URL construction, not message formatting or delivery contracts
- ✅ Channel contract unchanged — send/receive/status methods identical signatures
- ✅ Proven pattern — follows same URL resolution pattern used by Discord, Slack, Telegram channel plugins

**Security**:
- ✅ SSRF protections remain fully in place
- ✅ No new config surfaces that could be misconfigured

## Current review state

- Codex review requested real behavior proof — addressed above with screenshots and structured evidence fields
- All known concerns addressed: proof, compatibility, message delivery safety

target.title: feat(durable): add durable session task runtime foundation
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

This PR adds the opt-in, local-first durable runtime foundation proposed by PR1. The target failure mode is coordinator silence: long-running session/task/subagent work can continue across many steps, branches, and process restarts, but operators and runtime code need a bounded durable projection of which run, step, child, signal, or recovery state is open.

This is not a general-purpose workflow engine and does not include Work module, Workboard UI/tools, Task Flow projection adapters, or product-specific logic.

## Dependency Chain

This is PR2 in the replacement durable runtime stack:

1. PR1: durable session/task runtime RFC v2.
2. PR2: durable runtime foundation, this PR.
3. PR3: agent/session/subagent wiring on top of this foundation.

This PR is designed to be reviewable independently as a core foundation slice.

## Summary

Adds:

- `durable_runtime_*` tables in the shared OpenClaw state DB;
- SQLite store lifecycle with schema version checks and shared state permission hardening;
- runtime runs, steps, events, refs, links, timers, and signals;
- local-first claim/release, heartbeat, recovery, and bounded worker helpers;
- read-only CLI and Gateway inspection surfaces;
- generic coordination projection with unsupported write controls disabled;
- Kysely generated types and guardrails for the new schema;
- public CLI docs for enablement, env vars, storage, and input retention.

## Explicit Non-Scope

- Work module behavior.
- Workboard UI/tools.
- Task Flow projection adapters.
- Retention/compaction policy.
- Postgres/multi-worker lease contention.
- Automatic retry/resume policy.
- Ledger-only write controls.

## Latest Reviewer Follow-Up

Updated on 2026-07-02 after rebasing onto upstream `origin/main` commit `133ce01e4a`.

Head: `3e39e28135d81586a2851bc68f5d554527ac70d0`.

Addressed ClawSweeper P1 findings:

- Recovery reconciliation now honors the documented explicit worker opt-in. `startDurableRecoveryWorker` uses the shared `OPENCLAW_DURABLE_WORKER` gate, so `OPENCLAW_DURABLE_RUNTIME=1` alone remains an inspection/recording mode and does not start reconciliation.
- Future durable schema detection now runs immediately after `durable_schema_migrations` is available and before any `durable_runtime_*` table DDL, ALTER, or backfill work.
- The branch was rebased onto current upstream main; GitHub now reports the PR as conflict-free.

Regression coverage added:

- `src/durable/recovery.test.ts` advances fake timers with durable runtime enabled and no worker flag, then asserts no shared SQLite state file is created.
- `src/durable/sqlite-store.test.ts` opens a DB stamped with a newer durable schema version, expects rejection, and verifies no `durable_runtime_*` tables were created before the throw.

## Evidence

Post-rebase validation:

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run --config test/vitest/vitest.unit.config.ts src/durable/recovery.test.ts src/durable/sqlite-store.test.ts src/durable/worker.test.ts src/durable/agent-turn.test.ts src/durable/subagent.test.ts src/durable/fan-in.test.ts`

- disabled CLI inspection returning the disabled message without creating durable state files;
- enabled CLI inspection creating/opening `<temp>/state/openclaw.sqlite`;

target.title: Plugins: enforce private import boundaries
target.body:
## Summary

- Problem: Plugins could couple directly to private OpenClaw internals or escape their package root through imports, even though the intended contract is the plugin SDK seam.
- Why it matters: That makes plugin behavior depend on unstable host internals and weakens the architecture boundary between plugin code and core.
- What changed: Added an enforced loader-time import policy that allows `openclaw/plugin-sdk/*`, declared package dependencies, Node builtins, and in-package relative imports, while blocking private `openclaw/*` imports, undeclared bare packages, and imports that escape the plugin root.
- What did NOT change (scope boundary): This does not add process isolation or a sandbox; plugins still run arbitrary JS in-process.

- [x] Feature
- [x] Security hardening

## Scope (select all touched areas)

- [x] API / contracts
- [x] Integrations

## Linked Issue/PR

- Closes #
- Related #

## User-visible / Behavior Changes

- Third-party and bundled plugins now fail to load when they import private OpenClaw package paths, undeclared bare packages, or files outside their own package root.
- Plugin authors can continue using declared dependencies, Node builtins, and `openclaw/plugin-sdk/*` seams.

## Security Impact (required)

- New permissions/capabilities? (`Yes/No`) No
- Secrets/tokens handling changed? (`Yes/No`) No

target.body:
## Summary

- Problem: OpenClaw had no built-in isolated rescue watchdog that could detect an unhealthy managed gateway profile and repair it without going through the failing primary session.
- Why it matters: the larger rescue-watchdog feature is hard to review as one PR; this split lands the core runtime/service layer first so maintainers can review the actual watchdog mechanism without onboarding/UI noise.
- What changed: adds daemon/service hardening needed by the watchdog, introduces a new isolated `rescueWatchdog` cron payload + runner, and wires the gateway cron service to execute that watchdog job against a monitored profile.
- What did NOT change (scope boundary): no onboarding wizard flow, no CLI `openclaw onboard --rescue-watchdog` UX, and no docs changes in this PR.

## Change Type (select all)

## User-visible / Behavior Changes

- Adds a new internal isolated cron payload kind, `rescueWatchdog`, for watchdog jobs that monitor a target profile and repair it when unhealthy.
- Hardens LaunchAgent plist writes: trusted-home resolution, symlink rejection, atomic writes, and `0600` plist permissions.

  The new capability is intentionally narrow: an isolated cron job can probe and repair a monitored local profile. Risk is bounded by restricting the payload shape, disallowing delivery targets for `rescueWatchdog`, resolving the monitored profile explicitly, and hardening the underlying managed-service restart and launchd plist write paths. The repair fallback uses exact argv via `process.execPath` and avoids shell-based PATH resolution.

## Repro + Verification

### Environment

- OS: macOS
- Runtime/container: Node 22 / pnpm workspace
- Model/provider: N/A
- Integration/channel (if any): N/A

  - `AbortSignal` now propagates through launchd/systemd/schtasks restart helpers into the process exec layer.
  - `rescueWatchdog` cron payloads normalize correctly, are forced to isolated session targets, and reject delivery/failureDestination config.
  - the rescue watchdog runner probes the monitored profile, attempts managed service restart, falls back to `doctor --repair --non-interactive`, and reports success/error summaries correctly.

target.title: fix(acpx): validate parsed PIDs with Number.isFinite in parseProcessList
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`parseProcessList` applies `Number.parseInt` to PID and PPID values extracted from `ps` output without validating the parsed result. While the current regex (`\d+`) captures only digits, a future regex change could produce `NaN` values that propagate to `process.kill()`, which throws on non-finite PID arguments.

This is the same class of issue that PR #98371 fixed in `src/cli/ports.ts`. The same `isValidPid()` pattern exists in `src/shared/pid-alive.ts`, but as per the extension boundary rules, this fix uses `Number.isFinite` directly inline.

## Why This Change Was Made

Defensive programming: catch malformed PID/PPID values at parse time rather than relying on downstream guards (`uniquePids` filters `Number.isInteger(pid) && pid > 0`, but NaN might bypass that check in unexpected code paths). Consistent with the pattern applied in PR #98371.

## User Impact

None on correct `ps` output. The regex still requires digit-only pid/ppid groups, so all valid process entries pass through unchanged. Invalid (non-finite) entries are silently skipped, matching the existing behavior of skipping non-matching lines.

## Evidence

**Tests pass**: all 146 ACPX extension tests pass (13 test files):
```
Test Files  13 passed (13)
Tests  146 passed (146)
```

**Before (current main)**:
- `parseProcessList` pushes entries without pid/ppid validation
- Despite regex guard, NaN from a hypothetical malformed line would reach downstream processing

**After (this fix)**:
- `Number.parseInt` result validated with `Number.isFinite` before use
- Invalid entries are skipped (continue), same pattern as non-matching line handling
- Existing behavior preserved for all valid inputs

**Verification**: The `parseProcessList` function is tested indirectly through `listPlatformProcesses` which is invoked via the mocked `listProcesses` dependency in `cleanupOpenClawOwnedAcpxProcessTree` tests. All existing test scenarios (valid process entries, orphan detection, tree traversal, lease identity) pass unchanged.

target.title: fix: harden formatCurrencyAmount, formatCoords, and record code-mode bridge rejections
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Three defensive hardening changes across location formatting, DeepSeek usage formatting, and code-mode bridge promise handling. The gateway-lock handle leak has been dropped (covered by #98848).

## Why This Change Was Made

### 1. Record rejected code-mode bridge promises at pending-state creation boundary

`createPendingBridgeStates` attached a fulfillment-only `.then((settled) => state.settled = settled)` to each bridge promise. A rejection would surface as unhandledRejection through the bare .then(onFulfilled) pattern.

**Fix:** Added `.then(onFulfilled, onRejected)` in `createPendingBridgeStates` that records `{ ok: false, error }` in entry.settled at creation time. Simplified `waitForPending` since individual promises already have rejection handlers.

### 2. Guard `formatCurrencyAmount` against non-finite amounts

`formatCurrencyAmount` calls `amount.toFixed(2)` without `Number.isFinite(amount)`. NaN produces "$NaN" which is misleading to users.

### 3. Guard `formatCoords` against NaN/Infinity coordinates

`formatCoords` calls `latitude.toFixed(6)` without `Number.isFinite` guard. NaN renders as "NaN, NaN" instead of a meaningful value.

## User Impact

- **code-mode**: Prevents unhandledRejection from late-rejecting bridge promises. Error is preserved in settled state for downstream.
- **DeepSeek/location**: Defensive hardening — produces "unknown" instead of misleading "NaN"/"Infinity" strings.

target.title: fix(llm): skip native DeepSeek V4 wrapper for OpenRouter routes
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

DeepSeek V4 models routed through OpenRouter (`openrouter/deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash`, `openrouter/deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro`) reject every request with:

```
400 "reasoning_effort" and "reasoning.effort" are both provided with conflicting values
```

Closes #97196.

## Why This Change Was Made

Two code paths emit reasoning-control fields and they disagree on the source of truth for `thinkingFormat`:

- `openai-completions.ts` chat-completions builder reads the **merged** compat from `getCompat(model)`, which auto-detects `thinkingFormat: "openrouter"` for any `provider === "openrouter"` model and emits `reasoning: { effort }`.
- The DeepSeek V4 stream wrapper (`extra-params.ts` `isDeepSeekV4OpenAICompatibleModel`) gates only on the user-config compat (`model.compat.thinkingFormat`), which stays `undefined` even after auto-detection. The wrapper then fires and writes `reasoning_effort`, so the request ends up with both fields and DeepSeek returns HTTP 400.

The wrapper already excludes `microsoft-foundry` provider ids. This change extends that pattern to OpenRouter-routed models, matching the existing exclusion semantics and the documented OpenRouter route for DeepSeek V4 (`docs/providers/openrouter.md`).

## User Impact

- OpenRouter-routed DeepSeek V4 calls no longer fail with HTTP 400; only `reasoning: { effort }` is sent (the OpenRouter-supported shape).
- Other providers (canonical DeepSeek, Microsoft Foundry, Azure Foundry via `thinkingFormat: "openai"`, ZAI, Qwen) keep their existing behavior.

target.title: fix: support Claude Sonnet 5 adaptive thinking requests
target.body:
Closes #98386
Related: #98254

## What Problem This Solves

Claude Sonnet 5 uses Anthropic adaptive thinking semantics. Requests that still look like older manual-thinking payloads, or that include non-default sampling / priority service-tier fields, can fail against the Anthropic API.

This PR keeps the fix scoped to Anthropic-family request paths so OpenClaw can send Claude Sonnet 5 requests with the provider contract Sonnet 5 expects.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Sonnet 5 default and explicit `adaptive` thinking send native adaptive thinking without forcing `output_config.effort`.
- Explicit `low` and other effort levels send adaptive thinking with the requested Anthropic effort.
- Explicit `off` disables thinking for Sonnet 5 where the Anthropic API allows it.

Users can configure Claude Sonnet 5 through the existing OpenClaw thinking controls:

- no explicit setting: Sonnet 5 uses Anthropic adaptive thinking by default
- `adaptive`: sends Anthropic adaptive thinking without an effort override
- `low`: sends Anthropic adaptive thinking with low effort

target.title: fix(agents): preserve fresh tool result text under aggregate cap
target.body:
Closes #98874
Related: #96857

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users in long-lived WebChat, Discord, or other direct agent sessions could see fresh text tool outputs such as `exec`, `read`, `browser`, or `session_status` degrade into `(see attached image)` or otherwise disappear from the model-visible prompt when aggregate tool-result history was already saturated.

## Why This Change Was Made

Prompt-history tool-result truncation now protects the trailing fresh tool-result batch first, then recovers aggregate budget from older projected history before falling back to trimming the fresh batch only when that batch itself exceeds the aggregate cap. Aggregate elision now uses a budget-bounded marker so the recovery plan cannot claim success while leaving counted tool-result text above the configured budget.

This stays scoped to the live prompt projection path; persisted session truncation and preemptive recovery estimates keep their existing aggregate-budget behavior.

## User Impact

Agents can inspect small fresh command/file/status outputs even after old session history has filled the aggregate tool-result budget. Oversized or multi-tool fresh batches remain bounded, so context-overflow protection still applies without turning ordinary new text into an image-only placeholder.

## Evidence

- Reproduced the root class locally with a focused regression test: a saturated history projection followed by fresh `ABC` output previously risked clearing the fresh result; the new test preserves `ABC` while keeping total tool-result text within the 32k aggregate cap.
- Added coverage for oversized fresh trailing results, multi-tool fresh batches over the aggregate cap, and tiny explicit aggregate budgets where elision markers themselves must fit the budget.
- PR-head saturated prompt-history proof, run against branch `feature/issue-98874-tool-result-text` at `50069fdd6f`. target.title: fix(diagnostics): emit tool.execution.error for soft-error tool results
target.body:
Related: #55806

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators monitoring tool execution dashboards would see tools like `memory_search`, `composio_*`, `pages_*`, and `transcribe` reported as successful even when they returned error payloads (`status: unavailable`, `disabled: true`, `error: "…"`). The progress draft correctly showed these as failed (via `isToolResultError`), but OTEL/Prometheus telemetry counted them as `tool.execution.completed`, making error-rate dashboards unreliable.

## Why This Change Was Made

The diagnostic emit path in `wrapToolWithBeforeToolCallHook` only classified tool failures by caught exceptions (`catch` branch → `tool.execution.error`). Tools that return soft-error results without throwing were unconditionally emitted as `tool.execution.completed`. The stream observer already used `isToolResultError(result)` from `tool-result-error.ts` to detect these — this change reuses the same predicate in the telemetry emit path so both classifications agree.

The `errorCategory` is derived from `readToolResultStatus(result)` (the normalized `details.status` string, e.g. `"unavailable"`, `"disabled"`, `"timeout"`), falling back to `"ToolReportedError"` when no status is present but other error signals match (`ok: false`, `Boolean(details.error)`, non-zero `exitCode`).

## User Impact

Tool execution error dashboards (Grafana/Prometheus panels filtering on `openclaw_errorCategory != ""`) will now correctly surface soft-error tool calls. No change to agent behavior or user-facing tool output — only the diagnostic telemetry classification changes.

## Evidence

- New test: `"emits tool.execution.error when execute returns a soft-error result without throwing"` — mocks a tool returning `{ details: { status: "unavailable", disabled: true, error: "…" } }` and asserts that the emitted event is `tool.execution.error` with `errorCategory: "unavailable"` (not `tool.execution.completed`).

target.title: Support Ultra thinking for the native Codex runtime
target.body:
## Summary

Adds `ultra` as a first-class thinking level for OpenClaw's **native Codex app-server runtime** when the live Codex model catalog advertises that level.

This is intentionally not a generic `ultra -> max` alias. Native Codex owns the full Ultra semantics: proactive multi-agent orchestration plus backend-compatible maximum inference effort. Embedded OpenClaw/provider runtimes that do not implement that orchestration do not advertise Ultra.

Legacy aliases remain stable: `ultrathink` continues to normalize to `high`; only explicit `ultra` selects the new tier.

## What Problem This Solves

OpenAI Codex PR <https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/29899> defines Ultra as a user-facing orchestration level:

- Codex Core selects `MultiAgentMode::Proactive`.
- Codex injects proactive delegation instructions and owns native sub-agent execution.
- At inference boundaries, Codex maps Ultra to the backend-compatible `max` effort.

Therefore OpenClaw should pass explicit `ultra` unchanged to the native Codex app-server, not flatten it to `max` itself. Other OpenClaw runtimes must not claim Ultra support merely because they can send `max`.

## Changes

- Add `ultra` to canonical thinking-level/session types needed to carry a native Codex selection.
- Preserve `ultrathink -> high` for backwards compatibility; explicit `ultra` is required.
- Expose Ultra only from the native Codex provider profile when live app-server discovery advertises it.
- Pass `effort: "ultra"` through native Codex `turn/start` and collaboration-mode settings.
- Keep embedded OpenClaw/OpenAI/Google/Anthropic provider profiles Ultra-free unless they separately implement equivalent orchestration semantics.
- Add tests for normalization, Codex profile discovery, native request payloads, unsupported-runtime rejection/clamping, and legacy alias behavior.
- Update thinking-level documentation with the native-Codex-only scope.

## Evidence

### Official semantics

OpenAI Codex PR <https://github.com/openai/codex/pull/29899> implements Ultra in Codex Core. Its source derives proactive multi-agent mode from `ReasoningEffort::Ultra`, injects proactive delegation instructions, and converts Ultra to `max` only at inference request boundaries.

### Real configured-provider behavior (sanitized)

Codex CLI 0.142.4 was configured with:

```toml
model = "gpt-5.6-sol"
model_reasoning_effort = "ultra"
```

Live model discovery advertised:

```text
gpt-5.6-sol: low, medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra
```

target.title: fix(config): reload changes from included files
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The Gateway hot-reloader watched only `openclaw.json`. Changes made directly to successfully resolved `$include` files could leave the running Gateway on stale configuration until the root file changed or the process restarted.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Carries canonical include paths from successful guarded reads through the internal metadata wrapper without changing the public `ConfigFileSnapshot` or `config.get` shape.
- Starts a singleton root watcher plus exact-file watchers for the last valid nested include graph.
- Stages graph replacements until every new watcher is ready, keeps the prior set live during handoff, reconciles once after readiness, and uses bounded retry with polling fallback.
- Keeps invalid snapshots on the last valid watch set, bypasses only root-write hash dedupe for include events, and prevents rejected hot reloads from being replayed or promoted.
- Documents the supported behavior and its intentional discovery limits.

## User Impact

Edits to valid, already resolved include files now trigger Gateway config reloads, including nested includes and authored `$include` target changes inside watched files.

Paths that were missing or invalid during the last successful resolution, plus filesystem or symlink retargets that do not modify a watched file, still require an `openclaw.json` edit or Gateway restart.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/config-reload.test.ts src/gateway/server-reload-handlers.test.ts src/gateway/server-startup-config.recovery.test.ts` — 8 files / 410 tests passed after rebase.

target.title: feat(bedrock): enable prompt caching for Nova models
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes #29707. Amazon Nova generation models on Bedrock were still treated as unsupported non-Anthropic models, so OpenClaw forced `cacheRetention: "none"` and never emitted Bedrock `cachePoint` blocks for Nova requests.

## Why This Change Was Made

AWS documents explicit prompt caching support for Amazon Bedrock models, including Nova generation models: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-caching.html

This change teaches the shared Bedrock cache policy to recognize Nova Micro, Lite, Pro, Premier, and Nova 2 Lite refs, lets direct Nova requests keep their cache settings, and keeps the existing no-cache fallback for unsupported non-Anthropic Bedrock models. For Nova, `cacheRetention: "long"` emits the default Bedrock cache point without reusing Claude's `ttl: "1h"` field.

The follow-up commit also preserves configured direct Nova `cacheRetention` values through the normal agent extra-params path, including the explicit `cacheRetention: "none"` opt-out.

## User Impact

Users can enable prompt caching for Bedrock Nova text models without hitting the previous runtime no-cache override. Unsupported non-Anthropic Bedrock models, such as Mistral, continue to be protected from unsupported cache metadata.

target.title: fix(browser): bound Playwright response body reads to prevent OOM
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`responseBodyViaPlaywright` in `extensions/browser/src/browser/pw-tools-core.responses.ts` previously used `resp.text()` which loads the entire response as a JavaScript string (unbounded memory allocation) before checking `maxChars`. On a 500 MB response this allocated 500 MB+ before truncation.

Playwright's `Response` API doesn't expose streaming — both `body()` and `text()` buffer the full payload. Truly bounded capture requires CDP-level `Fetch.takeResponseBodyAsStream`.

## Why This Change Was Made

Replaced `resp.text()` (and `resp.body()`) with a dual-path architecture:

1. **CDP `Fetch.takeResponseBodyAsStream` (primary, Chromium):** `Fetch.enable` → `Fetch.requestPaused` → `Fetch.takeResponseBodyAsStream` → `IO.read` 64KB chunks → `IO.close` at cap → `Fetch.fulfillRequest` to deliver response to page. Default cap: 800 KB (= maxChars 200K × 4 UTF-8 max). No full-response Buffer allocation. Page navigation completes normally via fulfillRequest.

2. **`body()`+`subarray()` fallback (Firefox/WebKit):** Falls through when `newCDPSession()` fails. Uses `resp.body()` but decodes only `buf.subarray(0, maxBytes)` to avoid full-string allocation.

This eliminates the OOM risk from large Playwright responses while keeping backward compatibility for all existing callers.

## User Impact

- **No user-visible behavior change** — oversized responses still return truncated prefix matching `maxChars`. URL, status, and headers are returned unchanged.
- **Memory improvement:** CDP streaming allocates only 832 KB vs 20 MB+ for the old path on a 10 MB response.
- **Larger responses see proportionally larger savings** since CDP always caps at ~832 KB regardless of response size.
- **Firefox/WebKit users** see the same behavior as before (fallback path with `body()`+`subarray()` but no full-string decode).
- **Page navigation completes** — `Fetch.fulfillRequest` delivers the response to the page with original status/headers (empty body since stream was consumed), verified in real browser proof.

## Evidence

### Real browser proof (required for external PRs)

Real Google Chrome 138 headless, real HTTP server with 10 MB response:

```
=== MEMORY COMPARISON ===
| Method                  | Data buffered   | Output  | Page OK? | Bounded? |
|-------------------------|-----------------|---------|----------|----------|
| CDP Fetch stream        | 832 KB           | 200K ch | YES      | YES      |
| resp.body()+toString()  | 10.00MB Buffer + 10.00MB str | 200K ch | YES      | NO       |
| Memory reduction        | 25x                        |         |          |          |
```

- **CDP streaming** reads only **832 KB** (maxBytes=800K + one extra 64KB chunk) — truly bounded.
- **Page load completed: YES** — `Fetch.fulfillRequest` delivers a response to the page so navigation completes.
- **Old `resp.body()`+`toString()`** allocates **20 MB** (10 MB Buffer + 10 MB string) — still unbounded.
- **25× memory reduction** on a 10 MB response; for larger responses (100 MB+, e.g. generated HTML pages) the reduction is proportionally larger since CDP always caps at ~832 KB.

Full log: `docs/.local/issue-browser-bound-reads/cdp-streaming-proof.log`

### Negative control (proves the OLD unbounded behavior)

```
[browser response bounded-read negative control] old text() path: buffered=1000000 chars
```

The old `resp.text()` path loads **1,000,000 characters** before checking `maxChars=10`. The fix caps decode at maxBytes.

### Mutation test (proves bounded decode is load-bearing)

```
[browser response bounded-read mutation test] UNBOUNDED (no subarray): decoded=500000 chars
```

Removing the `subarray()` decode window would decode **500,000 chars** instead of **40** with the fix.

## Tests and validation

- **19 tests pass** (15 original + 4 new CDP path tests):
  - CDP stream reads full body when under cap
  - CDP stream truncates at maxBytes cap (IO.read stops early)
  - Non-matching URL continued immediately without body read
  - Falls back to body()+subarray when CDP session unavailable
  - CDP stream uses `Fetch.fulfillRequest` to preserve page response delivery
  - Negative control with old text() path
  - Mutation test proving subarray is load-bearing
- **TypeScript compiles cleanly** (`pnpm tsgo:core`)

## Risk checklist

- **User-visible behavior change?** No — oversized responses still return truncated prefix.
- **Config/env/migration change?** No.
- **Security/auth/network change?** No — CDP is a debug-protocol optimization; response metadata unchanged.
- **Highest-risk area:** CDP session creation failing mid-flight — handled via try/catch + fallback to body()+subarray (unchanged behavior for non-Chromium).
- **Page response delivery:** After CDP body is consumed, `Fetch.fulfillRequest` sends original status/headers to the page, verified in real browser proof.

## Linked context

Pattern from PR #98496 (bounded response body reads to prevent OOM).

target.title: fix(sessions): log warning when parseJsonlEntries skips malformed JSONL lines
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Three JSONL reader functions in session-manager.ts silently skip malformed transcript lines with bare catch blocks and zero diagnostic output. When a transcript file is corrupted, entries vanish with no operator visibility — no log, no warning, no metric.

This adds counted malformed-line detection and a single `logWarn` summary to all three readers: `parseJsonlEntries` (session load), `buildSessionInfo` (session listing), and `parseSessionEntries` (CLI history, BTW continuation, fork-source, embedded file state).

## Why This Change Was Made

Data loss without observability is the worst failure mode. The write side was hardened (`serializeJsonLine` throws on non-serializable roots), but transcripts already on disk from older code remain vulnerable. This adds the reader-side visibility so operators can detect and act on corruption.

## Evidence

### Committed test proof

Three test cases cover the warning behavior:

- `parseSessionEntries > logs a warning and skips malformed JSONL lines while preserving valid entries`
- `parseSessionEntries > reports the correct skip count for multiple malformed lines`
- `parseSessionEntries > parseJsonlEntries logs warning for malformed lines via loadEntriesFromFile`

### Local test run — 53/53 passed

```
pnpm test src/agents/sessions/session-manager.test.ts

 ✓ parseSessionEntries > parses valid JSONL lines without logging warnings 1ms
 ✓ parseSessionEntries > logs a warning and skips malformed JSONL lines while preserving valid entries 1ms
 ✓ parseSessionEntries > reports the correct skip count for multiple malformed lines 1ms
 ✓ parseSessionEntries > skips empty lines without counting them as malformed 1ms
 ✓ parseSessionEntries > parseJsonlEntries logs warning for malformed lines via loadEntriesFromFile 2ms
 ... (all 53 tests passing)

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  53 passed (53)
```

### What changed

- `session-manager.ts`: replaced bare `catch {}` in `parseJsonlEntries`, `buildSessionInfo`, and `parseSessionEntries` with counted skip + single `logWarn` summary
- `session-manager.test.ts`: added warning regression tests for all three readers

Low. Adds a single log line per corrupted transcript load. No change to valid-file behavior. Operator action is voluntary — the warning is informational.

target.title: feat(slack): add ignoreOtherMentions channel config
target.body:
## Summary

- Add `ignoreOtherMentions` option for Slack channel config, mirroring the existing Discord guild/channel feature
- When enabled, messages that mention another user (`<@U...>`) but do not explicitly mention the bot are dropped — even inside bot-participated threads
- This prevents the bot from replying when a user is talking to a coworker in a thread where the bot previously responded

## Slack vs Discord difference

Discord's `ignoreOtherMentions` checks `!wasMentioned && !implicitMention`. The Slack version intentionally omits the `!implicitMention` check because Slack's implicit mention (via `hasSlackThreadParticipation`) fires for **every** message in any bot-participated thread, which would make the feature ineffective.

## Config example

```json5
{
  channels: {
    slack: {
      channels: {
        "*": { ignoreOtherMentions: true },
      },
    },
  },
}
```

## Changed files

| File | Change |
|------|--------|
| `src/config/types.slack.ts` | Add `ignoreOtherMentions` to `SlackChannelConfig` |
| `src/config/zod-schema.providers-core.ts` | Add zod validation for the new field |
| `extensions/slack/src/monitor/channel-config.ts` | Wire through type + resolver |
| `extensions/slack/src/monitor/message-handler/prepare.ts` | Drop logic before mention gating |

target.title: feat: add tools.fs.roots — per-agent filesystem roots with access modes
target.body:
## Summary

- Problem: `tools.fs.workspaceOnly` is binary, so operators cannot safely allow agents to read or write a specific host path outside the workspace without opening broader filesystem access.
- Why it matters: multi-tenant and shared-gateway deployments often need narrowly scoped access to shared data, context files, or mounted knowledge directories.
- What changed: added `tools.fs.roots`, an explicit allowlist of filesystem roots with per-root `kind` (`dir`/`file`) and `access` (`ro`/`rw`), wired through host-mode FS tools, `apply_patch`, local media loading, outbound local-media/reply-delivery paths, and prompt-image auto-load.
- Host-mode `read` operations now use pinned file-descriptor root-scoped reads (`readFileWithinRoot`/`openFileWithinRoot`) to close the TOCTOU gap between path validation and file open, in addition to the existing pre-guard.
- Sandbox outbound media delivery now explicitly ignores configured `tools.fs.roots`, preventing sandbox-generated attachments from being rejected when host-mode roots are configured.
- What did NOT change: sandbox mode still relies on Docker isolation and ignores `tools.fs.roots`; `exec` sandboxing is unchanged; `tools.allow` / `tools.deny` behavior is unchanged.

## Change Type (select all)

## Root Cause / Regression History (if applicable)

- Root cause: existing FS policy exposed only two modes for host paths: workspace-only or unrestricted.
- Missing capability: there was no way to express "this agent may read `/data/shared/context.md` but may not read the rest of the host".

- If unknown, what was ruled out: sandbox mode stays out of scope because sandbox tools resolve container paths, not host paths, and partial host-path enforcement there would create an inconsistent security model.

## Regression Test Plan (if applicable)

- Scenarios locked in:
  - lexical dir/file root matching and ro/rw enforcement
  - canonical-root precedence over alias roots for host-mode mutation paths
  - unlink/delete behavior preserving symlink-entry semantics while still respecting stricter canonical roots
  - roots precedence over `workspaceOnly` for host-mode FS access
  - sandbox-mode fallback still honoring `workspaceOnly`
  - rooted local image/PDF/reference-image loads outside the workspace
  - rooted outbound local-media and reply-delivery paths preserving file-vs-dir root semantics
  - rooted prompt-image auto-load outside the workspace

## User-visible / Behavior Changes

- New config surface: `tools.fs.roots` on global `tools.fs` and per-agent `tools.fs`.

target.title: fix(tools-manager): replace spawnSync extraction with safe extractArchive API
target.body:
## Summary

**Problem**: `tools-manager.ts` uses `spawnSync("unzip"/"tar")` for archive extraction without any size limits, entry caps, or timeout protection, making the process vulnerable to ZIP bombs / decompression bombs if a malicious or corrupted archive is provided.

**Solution**: Replace the synchronous spawnSync-based extraction with the safe `extractArchive` API from `@openclaw/fs-safe` (re-exported from `src/infra/archive.ts`), which enforces size limits, entry count caps, timeout, and path traversal protection.

**What changed**: Removed 5 functions and 3 unused imports; added a single `extractArchiveSafe` async wrapper with explicit limits (maxArchiveBytes: 100MB, maxExtractedBytes: 500MB, maxEntries: 1000, timeoutMs: 60000). Updated tests to mock the new API.

**What did NOT change**: Extraction behavior for legitimate archives, binary discovery and installation logic, error handling for unsupported archive formats.

---

## What Problem This Solves

**Problem**: The tool manager's archive extraction had no bounds on input size or output volume, creating a denial-of-service surface through decompression bombs.

**Why This Change Was Made**: The existing `@openclaw/fs-safe` infrastructure already provides all necessary protections -- reusing it is the correct pattern rather than re-implementing limits on raw spawnSync calls.

**User Impact**: No user-visible change. Tool binaries (fd/rg) continue to download and install as before. Users and operators gain protection against oversized or malicious archives.

---

## Root Cause

**Trigger condition**: Any download of a fd or ripgrep archive from GitHub releases (or any future tool) that is corrupted or maliciously oversized.

**Root cause analysis**: `extractTarGzArchive()` and `extractZipArchive()` in `tools-manager.ts` directly shelled out to system tar/unzip without any pre-flight size check, extraction budget, or timeout. OpenClaw had a safe archive layer but the tool manager bypassed it.

**Affected scope**: All platforms (Linux, macOS, Windows). Only the tool manager (src/agents/utils/tools-manager.ts) -- other extraction paths already use `@openclaw/fs-safe`.

---

## Linked context

- **Related analysis**: Defensive programming audit Section 3.4
- **In scope**: Replacement of extraction logic in tools-manager.ts
- **Out of scope**: Other extraction sites, linting of future spawnSync extraction patterns
- **Design doc**: docs/.local/defensive-archive-extraction/design.md

---

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: Safe archive extraction with size limits, entry caps, and timeout for tool manager downloads.

**Real environment tested**: Linux 4.19.112-2.el8.x86_64, Node 22, @openclaw/fs-safe@0.3.0

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
```bash
pnpm tsgo:core
pnpm test -- src/agents/utils/tools-manager.test.ts
```

**After-fix evidence**:
```
$ node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p tsconfig.core.json --incremental
(exit code 0, no errors)

 RUN  v4.1.8
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  5 passed (5)
```

**Observed result after the fix**: Type check passes with zero errors. All 5 unit tests pass. The extractArchive function from @openclaw/fs-safe is independently tested in src/infra/archive.test.ts with coverage for size limits, entry caps, symlink protection, and timeout.

**What was not tested**: Live download and extraction of actual fd/rg archives (requires network access to GitHub releases). The safe extraction API is the same code path used by src/infra/install-flow.ts which is already verified in production.

## Tests and validation

### Unit tests

```

 Test Files  1 passed (1)

```

### Integration / E2E

The @openclaw/fs-safe package's extractArchive is independently tested in src/infra/archive.test.ts for: archive size limits, entry count limits, symlink/hardlink traversal protection, absolute entry path rejection, staged extraction with safe merge.

## Risk checklist

- [x] This change has been tested with existing configurations

target.title: feat(agent): live claude-cli reasoning + progress preview
target.body:
Closes #97526

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users running a `claude-cli` live-session model with `/reasoning stream` would see a single reasoning bubble flash and disappear, followed by a long silent gap, and then the full answer arriving in one piece — instead of the continuously-updating live preview that the Codex app-server runtime gives for the same kind of turn on the same message-based channels (Telegram, Discord, etc.).

The two runtimes diverged on live UX even though the underlying data was identical: the bundled `claude-cli` backend already launches with `--output-format stream-json --include-partial-messages`, so Claude emits incremental `thinking_delta` blocks during extended thinking — they just weren't being consumed.

## Why This Change Was Made

The fix has three layers, each addressing a distinct break in the live-preview path:

1. **Parser (`src/agents/cli-output.ts`)** — the Claude stream-json JSONL parser only forwarded `text_delta` (assistant answer) and tool-use events; `thinking_delta` content blocks had no path, so reasoning surfaced as one transient block rather than a live stream. This change parses `content_block_delta` where `delta.type === "thinking_delta"` and forwards it through a new optional `onReasoningDelta` callback, accumulated separately from the answer text. Signature-only deltas are ignored.

2. **Auto-reply seam (`src/auto-reply/reply/agent-runner-*`)** — the CLI reasoning lane was being fed by a `claude-cli`-only hack that re-bridged the assistant answer text into the reasoning preview. That bridge is removed; the real `thinking` agent event now drives the reasoning lane, the same lane the embedded/Codex runtimes already use. The `/reasoning` visibility gate stays on this downstream seam.

3. **Progress compositor (`src/channels/progress-draft-compositor.ts`)** — keeps the reasoning preview live (tail-truncate + snapshot) and preserves the answer preview across the preamble boundary, so the channel renders incremental thinking and incremental answer without the preview collapsing.

Non-goals: no token-delta channel transport is introduced — this only feeds OpenClaw's existing message-based preview with deltas Claude already sends. Behavior for non-`claude-cli` providers is unchanged.

## Review answers ([P1] / [P2])

- **[P1] — the `/reasoning` gate must still suppress thinking when off.** The gate sits on the auto-reply seam (downstream of the parser), identical to the embedded runtime which already emits `stream:"thinking"` the same way. The source parser is left untouched — proven by the test below.
- **[P2] — turns that emit answer text but no `thinking_delta` must not lose the answer preview.** A no-thinking-delta fallback keeps the assistant answer preview alive — proven by the test below.

## User Impact

Users on `claude-cli` live-session models now get live reasoning progress in the channel preview during extended thinking, at parity with the Codex `progress` streaming experience: incremental thinking in the reasoning lane, incremental answer in the answer lane, no "blip → silence → final" gap. No configuration change is required.

## Evidence

Local run, consolidated branch `feat/claude-cli-thinking-stream` (5 commits, fast-forward).

**[P1] claude-cli thinking respects the `/reasoning` visibility gate**
`src/auto-reply/reply/agent-runner-execution.test.ts`
✓ does not bridge CLI thinking agent events to `onReasoningStream` when `silentExpected` is set (`/reasoning off` — parity with embedded runtime)
Proves the gate sits on the auto-reply seam (downstream), identical to the embedded runner which already emits `stream:"thinking"` the same way — source parser is left untouched.

**[P2] no-thinking-delta fallback keeps the answer preview alive**
`src/auto-reply/reply/agent-runner-execution.test.ts`
✓ preserves the assistant answer preview for claude-cli turns that emit assistant text but no `thinking_delta`

**Suite summary (vitest):**
1. claude-cli stream-json parser: `thinking_delta` routing — `src/agents/cli-output.test.ts` ✓
2. reasoning preview compositor (tail-truncate + snapshot) — Tests 3 passed (3)
3. auto-reply bridge: `/reasoning` gate + no-thinking fallback — Tests 217 passed (217)
4. telegram progress draft: preamble-preview preservation — Tests 136 passed (136)

Aggregate parser + compositor + timeline run:
`Test Files 3 passed (3) · Tests 267 passed (267)` · `oxlint rc=0`.

Changed files: `src/agents/cli-output.ts` (+ test), `src/agents/cli-runner/claude-live-session.ts`, `src/agents/cli-runner/execute.ts`, `src/auto-reply/reply/agent-runner-cli-dispatch.ts`, `src/auto-reply/reply/agent-runner-execution.ts` (+ test), `src/channels/progress-draft-compositor.ts` (+ timeline test), `extensions/telegram/src/bot-message-dispatch.ts` (+ test), `extensions/discord/src/monitor/message-handler.process.test.ts`.

target.title: fix(browser): bound Playwright response body reads to prevent OOM
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`responseBodyViaPlaywright` in `extensions/browser/src/browser/pw-tools-core.responses.ts` previously used `resp.text()` which loads the entire response as a JavaScript string (unbounded memory allocation) before checking `maxChars`. On a 500 MB response this allocated 500 MB+ before truncation.

Playwright's `Response` API doesn't expose streaming — both `body()` and `text()` buffer the full payload. Truly bounded capture requires CDP-level `Fetch.takeResponseBodyAsStream`.

## Why This Change Was Made

Replaced `resp.text()` (and `resp.body()`) with a dual-path architecture:

1. **CDP `Fetch.takeResponseBodyAsStream` (primary, Chromium):** `Fetch.enable` → `Fetch.requestPaused` → `Fetch.takeResponseBodyAsStream` → `IO.read` 64KB chunks → `IO.close` at cap → `Fetch.fulfillRequest` to deliver response to page. Default cap: 800 KB (= maxChars 200K × 4 UTF-8 max). No full-response Buffer allocation. Page navigation completes normally via fulfillRequest.

2. **`body()`+`subarray()` fallback (Firefox/WebKit):** Falls through when `newCDPSession()` fails. Uses `resp.body()` but decodes only `buf.subarray(0, maxBytes)` to avoid full-string allocation.

This eliminates the OOM risk from large Playwright responses while keeping backward compatibility for all existing callers.

## User Impact

- **No user-visible behavior change** — oversized responses still return truncated prefix matching `maxChars`. URL, status, and headers are returned unchanged.
- **Memory improvement:** CDP streaming allocates only 832 KB vs 20 MB+ for the old path on a 10 MB response.
- **Larger responses see proportionally larger savings** since CDP always caps at ~832 KB regardless of response size.
- **Firefox/WebKit users** see the same behavior as before (fallback path with `body()`+`subarray()` but no full-string decode).
- **Page navigation completes** — `Fetch.fulfillRequest` delivers the response to the page with original status/headers (empty body since stream was consumed), verified in real browser proof.

## Evidence

### Real browser proof (required for external PRs)

Real Google Chrome 138 headless, real HTTP server with 10 MB response:

```
=== MEMORY COMPARISON ===
| Method                  | Data buffered   | Output  | Page OK? | Bounded? |
|-------------------------|-----------------|---------|----------|----------|
| CDP Fetch stream        | 832 KB           | 200K ch | YES      | YES      |
| resp.body()+toString()  | 10.00MB Buffer + 10.00MB str | 200K ch | YES      | NO       |
| Memory reduction        | 25x                        |         |          |          |
```

- **CDP streaming** reads only **832 KB** (maxBytes=800K + one extra 64KB chunk) — truly bounded.
- **Page load completed: YES** — `Fetch.fulfillRequest` delivers a response to the page so navigation completes.
- **Old `resp.body()`+`toString()`** allocates **20 MB** (10 MB Buffer + 10 MB string) — still unbounded.
- **25× memory reduction** on a 10 MB response; for larger responses (100 MB+, e.g. generated HTML pages) the reduction is proportionally larger since CDP always caps at ~832 KB.

Full log: `docs/.local/issue-browser-bound-reads/cdp-streaming-proof.log`

### Negative control (proves the OLD unbounded behavior)

```
[browser response bounded-read negative control] old text() path: buffered=1000000 chars
```

The old `resp.text()` path loads **1,000,000 characters** before checking `maxChars=10`. The fix caps decode at maxBytes.

### Mutation test (proves bounded decode is load-bearing)

```
[browser response bounded-read mutation test] UNBOUNDED (no subarray): decoded=500000 chars
```

Removing the `subarray()` decode window would decode **500,000 chars** instead of **40** with the fix.

## Tests and validation

- **19 tests pass** (15 original + 4 new CDP path tests):
  - CDP stream reads full body when under cap
  - CDP stream truncates at maxBytes cap (IO.read stops early)
  - Non-matching URL continued immediately without body read
  - Falls back to body()+subarray when CDP session unavailable
  - CDP stream uses `Fetch.fulfillRequest` to preserve page response delivery
  - Negative control with old text() path
  - Mutation test proving subarray is load-bearing
- **TypeScript compiles cleanly** (`pnpm tsgo:core`)

## Risk checklist

- **User-visible behavior change?** No — oversized responses still return truncated prefix.
- **Config/env/migration change?** No.
- **Security/auth/network change?** No — CDP is a debug-protocol optimization; response metadata unchanged.
- **Highest-risk area:** CDP session creation failing mid-flight — handled via try/catch + fallback to body()+subarray (unchanged behavior for non-Chromium).
- **Page response delivery:** After CDP body is consumed, `Fetch.fulfillRequest` sends original status/headers to the page, verified in real browser proof.

## Linked context

Pattern from PR #98496 (bounded response body reads to prevent OOM).

target.title: feat: configurable default agent ID (escape the 'main' prison) 🦞
target.body:
## Summary

Adds support for overriding the hardcoded `"main"` fallback agent ID, so users with a single custom-named agent no longer get a ghost `agents/main/` default path/session identity when no `agents.list` is configured.

## The Problem

`DEFAULT_AGENT_ID` falls back to `"main"`. Some resolution paths run from partial config or before a full multi-agent list exists, so a setup that intends a custom default agent can still resolve the main session key and default agent directory as `main`.

## Solution

Two complementary override mechanisms:

### 1. Config key: `agents.defaultAgentId`

```json
{
  "agents": {
    "defaultAgentId": "maine-lobster"
  }
}
```

### 2. Env var: `OPENCLAW_DEFAULT_AGENT_ID`

```bash
export OPENCLAW_DEFAULT_AGENT_ID=maine-lobster
```

### Priority (highest → lowest)

1. `agents.list[].default: true` (explicit default agent)
2. `agents.list[0]` (first configured agent)
3. `agents.defaultAgentId` config key
4. `OPENCLAW_DEFAULT_AGENT_ID` env var
5. Hardcoded `"main"` (backward compatible)

## Changes

- Adds `agents.defaultAgentId` to the config schema/types and generated docs baseline.
- Updates `resolveDefaultAgentId()`, `listAgentIds()`, `resolveDefaultAgentDir()`, and main-session key resolution to honor config/env fallback values.
- Keeps populated `agents.list` behavior unchanged: list default/first entry still wins.
- Updates provider auth/default-agent directory resolution to use the effective default agent.
- Adds regression tests for config default, env fallback, default dir, and main-session key behavior.

## Testing

- `pnpm config:schema:check`
- `pnpm config:docs:check`
- `pnpm test src/agents/agent-scope-config.test.ts src/config/sessions/main-session.test.ts src/config/sessions/session-key.test.ts src/commands/auth-choice.test.ts src/commands/auth-choice.apply.plugin-provider.test.ts --maxWorkers=1`
- `pnpm check:changed`
- `git merge-tree --write-tree HEAD origin/main` → merge-clean

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed**: A config-only default agent ID should stop OpenClaw from falling back to the hardcoded `main` agent for the default agent directory and main session key.
- **Real environment tested**: Local OpenClaw checkout rebased onto latest `origin/main`, running the patched TypeScript source directly with Node/tsx in `/root/.openclaw/workspace/openclaw-pr-acpx/pr-51762`.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch**:

```console
$ node --import tsx --input-type=module <<'EOF'
import { resolveDefaultAgentId, resolveDefaultAgentDir } from './src/agents/agent-scope-config.ts';
import { resolveMainSessionKey } from './src/config/sessions/main-session.ts';
const cfg = { agents: { defaultAgentId: 'Ops Team' }, session: { mainKey: 'main' } };
const env = { OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR: '/tmp/openclaw-real-proof' };
console.log('defaultAgentId=' + resolveDefaultAgentId(cfg, env));
console.log('defaultAgentDir=' + resolveDefaultAgentDir(cfg, env));
console.log('mainSessionKey=' + resolveMainSessionKey(cfg, env));
EOF
```

```console
defaultAgentId=ops-team
defaultAgentDir=/tmp/openclaw-real-proof/agents/ops-team/agent
mainSessionKey=agent:ops-team:main
```

- **Observed result after fix**: `agents.defaultAgentId: "Ops Team"` is normalized to `ops-team`, the default agent directory resolves under `/tmp/openclaw-real-proof/agents/ops-team/agent`, and the main session key resolves to `agent:ops-team:main` instead of `main`.

target.title: fix(security): use constant-time comparison for TLS fingerprint verification
target.body:
## Summary

TLS certificate fingerprint verification in `src/gateway/client.ts` uses `!==` (standard JavaScript string equality), which is vulnerable to **timing side-channel attacks** (CWE-208).

An attacker on the network path can measure response time differences to iteratively guess the correct fingerprint byte-by-byte, potentially bypassing TLS pinning for MITM attacks on gateway connections.

## Root cause

Two locations perform fingerprint comparison with `!==`:

| Location | Context |
|----------|---------|
| Line 205 | WebSocket `checkServerIdentity` callback |
| Line 681 | HTTP `validateTlsFingerprint` method |

## Fix

Replace both with `safeEqualSecret()` from `src/security/secret-equal.ts`, which uses `SHA-256` hashing + `crypto.timingSafeEqual` for constant-time comparison.

This is the **same function already used** for pairing token verification elsewhere in the codebase — just missed for TLS fingerprints.

```diff
- if (fingerprint !== expected) {
+ if (!safeEqualSecret(fingerprint, expected)) {
```

## Why safeEqualSecret and not raw timingSafeEqual

`timingSafeEqual` requires both buffers to have equal length, which would leak the length of the expected fingerprint. `safeEqualSecret` avoids this by hashing both values with SHA-256 first (producing fixed 32-byte digests), then comparing the digests in constant time.

## Test plan

- [x] `pnpm tsgo` — compiles cleanly
- [x] `pnpm check` — lint/format passes
- [x] Existing `safeEqualSecret` tests in `src/security/audit-extra.sync.test.ts` cover equal, unequal, different-length, and undefined inputs
- [x] No remaining `fingerprint !== expected` patterns in codebase

target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Five test files create temporary directories with raw `fs.mkdtemp` / `fs.mkdtempSync` and never clean them up:

- `src/agents/models-config.providers.stepfun.test.ts`: 2 cases call `mkdtempSync` for agent auth-profile directories.
- `src/agents/models-config.providers.implicit.discovery-scope.test.ts`: 1 case calls `mkdtemp` for Google Vertex ADC credentials.
- `src/agents/agent-model-discovery.test.ts`: 1 case calls `fs.mkdtempSync` for an agent model directory.
- `src/agents/sessions/session-migrate-id-dedup.test.ts`: 2 cases call `mkdtempSync` for v1 session migration directories.
- `src/security/audit-config-include-perms.test.ts`: 1 case calls `fs.mkdtempSync` for a config-include permission audit directory.

These leaks add `/tmp` pressure across repeated test runs.

## Why This Change Was Made

Migrates all five files to the existing shared helper `createSuiteTempRootTracker` from `src/test-helpers/temp-dir.js`. The tracker creates one suite-level temp root in `beforeAll`, hands out isolated case subdirectories via `make()`, and removes the entire root in `afterAll`.

Changes per file:

- Replaced `mkdtemp` / `mkdtempSync` calls with `suiteTempDirs.make(...)`.
- Added `createSuiteTempRootTracker` import and `beforeAll` / `afterAll` setup/cleanup hooks.
- Removed now-unused `os` imports (and `node:fs`/`node:path` imports where they became unused).
- Kept all test bodies and assertions unchanged.

## User Impact

Test-only. Reduces dangling temp directories during agents and security test runs. No user-visible behavior change.

## Evidence

Unit tests:

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs \
```

target.title: ACP: add gateway-owned node-backed runtime
target.body:
## Summary

- Problem: OpenClaw did not yet have a complete **node-backed ACP runtime** where the gateway owns the durable state and a paired node acts only as the execution worker.
- Why it matters: without that split, restart/replay/reconnect behavior is too dependent on the live process, which makes lease fencing, terminal resolution, and outward delivery recovery harder to reason about and prove.
- What this PR adds:
  - a durable ACP gateway store for sessions, runs, accepted worker events, leases, terminal state, replay targets, and projector checkpoints
  - gateway ingestion of ACP worker events coming back from paired nodes
  - a real node-host ACP worker bridge and gateway/node command plumbing
  - a durable ACP reply projection/replay path so restart recovery can resume from gateway state instead of only from the live iterator
  - startup recovery for incomplete ACP node runs
  - restart/reconnect/cancel/close race hardening with focused restart/replay test coverage
  - architecture / protocol / verification docs for the new backend
- Landing-only follow-up: after rebasing onto current `main`, this PR also includes a few **test-only** isolation fixes in Feishu / Google / Google Chat extension tests that were needed to make the landing branch green. Those are not ACP runtime behavior changes.

## What changed by area

### 1) Durable ACP gateway state

New ACP store/state plumbing under `src/acp/store/**`:

- persists ACP sessions and runs
- persists accepted worker events
- tracks leases / lease epochs
- resolves canonical terminal state on the gateway
- stores replay targets and projector checkpoints separately from the runtime cursor

This is the foundation that lets the gateway stay authoritative even when execution happens on a paired node.

### 2) Gateway ↔ node ACP worker path

Main implementation areas:

- `src/gateway/**`
- `src/infra/node-commands.ts`
- `src/node-host/**`

This adds the node-backed ACP execution path:

- gateway can start/control ACP work on a paired node
- node-host can run the ACP worker role
- worker events stream back to the gateway over the existing node transport
- gateway remains the source of truth for run state and terminal resolution

### 3) Durable reply projection and replay

Main implementation areas:

- `src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-acp.ts`
- `src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-acp-delivery.ts`
- `src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-acp-replay.ts`

This PR moves ACP outward delivery onto a durable replayable path:

- reply targets are persisted per run
- projector checkpoints are advanced only after successful delivery
- restart recovery can replay the unfinished suffix from durable state
- reconnect and duplicate accepted events do not re-deliver already completed outward effects

### 4) Startup recovery / reconnect handling

Main implementation areas:

- `src/gateway/server-startup.acp-node.ts`
- `src/gateway/server-node-events.ts`
- `src/acp/runtime/acp-node.ts`

This adds the gateway-side recovery flow needed to:

- resume incomplete projection after restart
- keep reconnect handling deterministic
- prevent stale-worker wins
- preserve canonical terminal behavior across restart/replay windows

### 5) Test harnesses and regression coverage

Main test additions/expansions:

- `src/acp/store/store.restart.test.ts`
- `src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-acp.replay.test.ts`
- `src/gateway/server-startup.acp-node.test.ts`
- `src/gateway/server-node-events.acp.test.ts`
- `src/node-host/invoke-acp.test.ts`
- `src/acp/test-harness/restart-harness.ts`

These cover the core failure windows this backend needs to survive:

- restart after accepted events but before replay checkpoint advancement
- restart after terminal persistence but before final outward convergence
- reconnect replay of already accepted events
- cancel / complete / close race handling
- restart recovery with a real memory cut instead of reusing in-process objects

### 6) Docs included in this PR

Main docs:

- `docs/experiments/plans/acp-node-backed-runtime.md`
- `docs/experiments/plans/acp-node-backed-runtime-protocol.md`
- `docs/experiments/plans/acp-node-backed-runtime-verification.md`
- `docs/experiments/plans/acp-node-runtime-program.md`
- `docs/experiments/plans/acp-node-slice4-summary.md`
- `docs/experiments/plans/acp-node-slice4-final-judge.md`

These are included because this was developed as a staged architecture / verification effort and the final accepted behavior is documented there.

## Explicit scope boundaries / v1 limitations

This PR does **not**:

- turn nodes into mini-gateways
- add automatic cross-node continuation for an in-flight run
- claim durable resumed tool-message edit support after restart

Current conservative post-restart tool-update behavior remains:

- `append_only_after_restart`

## Change Type (select all)

- [x] Bug fix
- [x] Feature
- [ ] Refactor
- [x] Docs
- [ ] Security hardening
- [x] Chore/infra

## Scope (select all touched areas)
